tip: 'diye' can give a reason: 'gelecek diye mutluyum' means I'm happy that he'll come, marking the thought behind the feeling.
'yepyeni' intensifies the adjective: repeat the first sound of 'yeni' (new) with p to get brand new.
A polite request pairs the -ar/-er verb form with 'mı': 'bakar mısın' means could you check, softer than an order.
Turkish puts a describing clause before the noun with the -diği ending: 'gittiğimiz otel' means the hotel we went to.
For in order to, add 'için' after the -mek verb form: 'göndermek için' means in order to send, and the verb stays in dictionary form.
'gibi' means like and follows the noun it compares: 'pamuk gibi bulutlar' means clouds like cotton.
'hem... hem' frames two qualities together: 'hem sağlıklı hem ekonomik' means both healthy and economical.
For a past habit (used to), add -di to the -r form: 'temizlerdi' means she used to clean, a repeated routine.
Turkish states age with an 'at' ending: 'kaç yaşındasınız' is literally 'at what age are you', where 'yaşındasınız' carries -da (at).
The suffix -li on a place means from/of it: 'nerelisiniz' = nere-li (where-from), asking where are you from.
Doubling a word marks frequency: 'sık sık' means often, while 'sık' alone is dense. Repetition, not a plural.
A specific object takes the object ending -ı: 'arabanı' = araba-n-ı (your-car), marking it as the definite thing being parked.
The -er form states general facts, not one moment: 'gider' means goes as a rule, so this asks which bus normally serves the route.
'To be late' is 'geç kalmak', literally stay late: 'geç kaldınız' = you stayed late = you were late.
Negation -me- sits before the tense ending: 'izlemedim' = izle-me-di-m (watch-not-past-I), I did not watch.
The verb comes last in Turkish: 'hazırlar' (prepares) closes the sentence after subject 'annem' and object 'kahvaltı'.
Ability uses -abil-: 'kalabilir' = kal-abil-ir (stay-can), so 'kalabilir miyim' asks can I stay.
'Have' is expressed with 'var' (there is): 'ihtiyacım var' = my-need exists = I need it.
'X of Y' doubles up: the owner gets -ın, the thing gets -ı. 'kitabın yazarı' = of-the-book its-author = the book's author.
'yüzünden' means because of, used for a blamed or unwanted cause: 'komşular yüzünden' = because of the neighbors.
The -a/-e ending marks destination with motion verbs: 'restorana gitti' = went to the restaurant.
The suffix -ince/-ünce means when/once: 'çökünce' = once it descended, setting the trigger for the next action.
'en' before an adjective makes the 'most' form: 'en güzel' = most beautiful. Turkish has no separate -est ending.
-ken means while X-ing: 'yaparken' = while making, marking the background action during which something happens.
The -yordu- ending marks a was-doing action: 'konuşuyordum' = konuş-uyor-du-m (talk-ing-was-I), I was talking.
Need is shown with the -mam form plus 'lazım': 'kalkmam lazım' = my getting-up is necessary = I need to get up.
'From X to Y' pairs the -den ending (from) with '-e kadar' (up to): 'on birden on ikiye kadar' = from eleven to twelve.
Turkish says know how to with a verb-as-noun plus 'bilmek': 'yüzme biliyor musun' is literally do you know swimming.
For we need to, add -memiz to the verb before 'gerekiyor': 'değiştirmemiz gerekiyor', where -miz says it is us who must.
'şemsiyemi' stacks two suffixes: -m (my) then -i (the object), so 'şemsiye' becomes my umbrella as the object.
